source: No class sheet yet — these notes and questions are ours, written to Year 7 level. Grid references follow the class homework (4- and 6-figure, eastings first). When Finn's workbook pages are photographed, they can be added as class-sheet topics.

topics.title: Continents and oceans
topics.summary: The seven continents and five oceans, the Equator and the hemispheres — where everything is on a world map.

images.caption: The seven continents and five oceans. Russia is in both Europe and Asia — the Ural Mountains are the dividing line.

table.title: The seven continents, biggest first
head: Continent
Good to know
rows: Biggest continent, most people (China, India). Mount Everest.
Second biggest. The Equator crosses it. The Sahara Desert, the River Nile, Victoria Falls.
Canada, the USA, Mexico — and Greenland. The Grand Canyon.
Brazil, Argentina, Peru. The Amazon rainforest and the Andes mountains.
Around the South Pole. Coldest, windiest, iciest; no countries, only scientists.
The UK, France, Germany, Italy, Iceland … second smallest.
Also called Australia or Australasia: Australia, New Zealand, Pacific islands. Smallest.

facts: There are **7 continents** (huge areas of land) and **5 oceans** (huge areas of salt water).
Oceans, biggest first: **Pacific**, **Atlantic**, **Indian**, **Southern** (round Antarctica), **Arctic** (round the North Pole).
About **70%** of the Earth's surface is water.
The **Equator** is an imaginary line round the middle of the Earth (0° latitude). It splits the Earth into the **Northern** and **Southern Hemispheres**.
The **Prime Meridian** (0° longitude) runs from pole to pole through **Greenwich, London**. It splits east from west.
**Latitude** lines go across (east–west), like the rungs of a ladder. **Longitude** lines go from the North Pole to the South Pole.
The **UK** is in **Europe**, in the **Northern Hemisphere**, with the **Atlantic Ocean** to its west.

one of the 5 very large areas of salt water
a smaller area of salt water, often partly surrounded by land (e.g. the North Sea)

topics.title: Compass directions
topics.summary: The eight points of the compass, opposites, turning, and giving the direction from one place to another on a map.

images.caption: The 8 points of the compass. Clockwise from the top: Never Eat Shredded Wheat.

facts: The four **cardinal points** clockwise from the top: **North, East, South, West** — “**N**ever **E**at **S**hredded **W**heat”.
Halfway between them are **north-east, south-east, south-west, north-west**. North or south always comes first.
On most maps **north is at the top**. On OS maps the grid lines point north.
**“Which direction is B from A?”** — put your finger on **A** (the place after “from”) and look towards **B**.
Opposite directions are a **half turn (180°)** apart. A **quarter turn** is **90°**; one step round the 8-point compass is **45°**.
**Clockwise** goes N → NE → E → SE → S …; **anticlockwise** goes the other way.
The Sun **rises in the east** and **sets in the west**.
keywords: a tool whose needle points north (magnetic north)
north-east, south-east, south-west, north-west (also called ordinal points)
turning the same way as a clock's hands
turning the opposite way to a clock's hands

topics.title: Grid references
topics.summary: Finding places on a map with 4-figure grid references (a square) and 6-figure grid references (an exact point) — as in the class homework.

images.caption: A 4-figure grid reference names a square. Use its bottom-left corner: along the corridor to 25, up the stairs to 43 → 2543.
A 6-figure grid reference pinpoints a spot. Split the square into tenths: 25 and 4 tenths along (254), 43 and 7 tenths up (437) → 254437.

facts: Maps have a **grid** of squares. The lines going up the map are **eastings** — numbered **along the bottom** (and top); they get bigger going east.
The lines going across are **northings** — numbered **up the side**; they get bigger going north.
Always **eastings first**: “**along the corridor, then up the stairs**”.
A **4-figure** grid reference names a **square**: use the numbers of the lines that meet at its **bottom-left corner**.
A **6-figure** grid reference gives an **exact point**: imagine the square cut into **tenths**. The 3rd figure is tenths **along**, the 6th is tenths **up**.
You estimate the tenths by eye — halfway is 5. Being one tenth out is usually fine.
The **key** tells you what the **symbols** mean, e.g. a church, **PH** = pub (public house), **P** = post office, **Sch** = school.

the lines (and numbers) going along the map — read first
the lines (and numbers) going up the map — read second
pinpoints a place inside a square, e.g. 254437

questions.stem: In the grid reference 254437, what are the northings?
questions.explain: The last three figures are the northings: 43 and 7 tenths up → 437.

topics.title: Fantastic places
topics.summary: Seven fantastic places around the world — where they are, and how to describe a place like a geographer.

images.caption: Seven fantastic places. Can you name the continent each one is in?

table.title: Where are they?
head: Place
Continent
What makes it fantastic
rows: The world's biggest coral reef, home to thousands of kinds of sea life
The biggest tropical rainforest; the River Amazon carries more water than any other river
The biggest hot desert, across north Africa
The highest mountain on Earth: 8,849 m, in the Himalayas
A huge canyon cut by the Colorado River, more than 1.5 km deep
A giant waterfall on the Zambezi — “the smoke that thunders”
Volcanoes, geysers and glaciers — the land of fire and ice

facts: To **describe where a place is**, go from big to small: **continent → country → compass direction / nearby sea or city**.
Then describe its **physical features** (natural: mountains, rivers, climate, plants and animals) and its **human features** (made by people: towns, roads, tourism).
Use precise geography words: not “a big hill” but “a **mountain range**”; not “a hot sandy place” but “a **hot desert**”.
The biggest desert of all is **Antarctica** (a cold desert) — the **Sahara** is the biggest **hot** desert.
Many fantastic places are **World Heritage Sites**: places so special the world agrees to protect them.
keywords: a natural feature, e.g. a mountain, river, desert or reef
something made by people, e.g. a town, road or port
a thick forest with heavy rain all year
a place that gets very little rain (hot or cold)
a deep valley with steep sides, cut by a river
a place listed by UNESCO to be protected for everyone

topics.title: The Great Barrier Reef — why is it disappearing?
topics.summary: What the reef is, how coral lives, the threats that are killing it, and what is being done to protect it.

table.title: Why the reef is disappearing
head: Threat
What happens
rows: Coral bleaching: hot water makes coral push out its algae. It turns white and starves; if the heat lasts, it dies.
The sea absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic, so coral struggles to build its skeleton.
Rain washes soil, fertiliser and pesticide into the sea: cloudy water blocks sunlight and feeds pests.
Outbreaks of these starfish eat huge areas of coral.
Boat anchors, careless divers, overfishing and shipping damage the coral and its food chains.

facts: The **Great Barrier Reef** is off the **north-east coast of Australia** (Queensland), in the **Coral Sea**, part of the Pacific Ocean.
It is the **world's biggest coral reef system**: about **2,300 km** long, made of about **2,900 reefs** and **900 islands**. You can see it from space.
Coral is built by tiny animals called **polyps**. Tiny **algae** live inside them, making food from sunlight and giving coral its colours — so reefs need **warm, clear, shallow, sunny** water.
It is home to thousands of species — over **1,500 kinds of fish**, turtles, sharks, dolphins and dugongs — and it's a **World Heritage Site**.
The biggest threat is **climate change**: warmer seas cause **coral bleaching**. The reef has had several **mass bleaching** events since 2016.
**Bleached ≠ dead**: if the water cools quickly the algae can return. If the heat lasts, the coral dies — and a reef takes many years to recover.

**Protecting it:** marine park zones where fishing is banned, less farm run-off, removing crown-of-thorns starfish, growing and replanting coral — and, most of all, cutting the **greenhouse gases** that warm the planet.

the tiny animal that builds coral
tiny living things inside coral that make food from sunlight
coral turning white when the sea is too warm
long-term warming of the Earth, mainly from burning fossil fuels
the sea becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide
rainwater flowing off the land into rivers and the sea, carrying soil and chemicals
the variety of living things in a place

questions.stem: In which country is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: It's off the coast of Queensland, Australia.

questions.stem: Off which coast of Australia is the reef?
questions.explain: The reef runs along the north-east coast, in the Coral Sea.

questions.stem: Which sea is the Great Barrier Reef in?
questions.explain: The Coral Sea is part of the Pacific Ocean.

questions.stem: About how long is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: About 2,300 km — further than from London to Moscow. It's the largest coral reef system in the world.

questions.stem: What are the tiny animals that build coral called?
questions.explain: Coral polyps build hard limestone skeletons; over thousands of years these build up into a reef.

questions.stem: What tiny living things live inside coral, giving it food and its colours?
questions.explain: Algae inside the coral use sunlight to make food (photosynthesis) and share it with the coral.

questions.stem: What is it called when coral turns white because the sea is too warm?
questions.explain: In water that's too warm, coral pushes out its algae, loses its colour and turns white — bleaching.

questions.stem: What causes coral bleaching?
choices: Too much rain on the reef
questions.explain: Rising sea temperatures, caused by climate change, are the main cause of bleaching.

questions.stem: What is the biggest threat to the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: Climate change warms the sea (bleaching) and makes it more acidic. Other threats add to the damage.

questions.stem: Bleached coral is always dead.
questions.explain: Bleached coral is starving but alive. If the water cools quickly the algae can return; if the heat lasts too long, it dies.

questions.stem: Why does the sea become more acidic?
questions.answer: It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
choices: Rain washes salt out of it
questions.explain: The oceans soak up carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels. More acidic water makes it harder for coral to build its skeleton.

questions.stem: Which animal eats coral and has damaged large parts of the reef?
questions.explain: Outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish eat huge areas of coral. Divers remove them to protect the reef.

questions.stem: How does run-off from farms harm the reef?
questions.answer: Soil and fertiliser wash into the sea, making it cloudy and feeding pests
choices: Farm animals swim out and eat the coral
It makes the sea too cold
questions.explain: Rain washes soil, fertiliser and pesticides off farms in Queensland into rivers and the sea. Cloudy water blocks sunlight, and fertiliser helps crown-of-thorns starfish.

questions.stem: Why do coral reefs need clear, shallow water?
questions.answer: The algae inside the coral need sunlight to make food
choices: So that tourists can see them
questions.explain: Sunlight has to reach the algae for photosynthesis — that's why reefs grow in warm, clear, shallow, sunny seas.

questions.stem: Coral reefs grow best in cold, deep, dark water.
questions.explain: Reef-building coral needs warm, clear, shallow water with plenty of sunlight.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef is so big it can be seen from space.
questions.explain: Yes — it's the biggest structure made by living things on Earth.

questions.stem: Which of these helps to protect the reef?
questions.answer: Banning fishing in some zones of the marine park
choices: Building more ports on the reef
questions.explain: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park has zones where fishing is banned; there are also rules on farm run-off, starfish culls and coral replanting. Cutting greenhouse gases worldwide helps most of all.

questions.stem: Why does the reef matter to people as well as wildlife?
questions.answer: Tourism brings money and jobs, and the reef protects the coast from waves
choices: It stops it raining in Australia
It makes the sea fresh water
It keeps sharks away from Europe
questions.explain: Millions of visitors bring money and tens of thousands of jobs; the reef also breaks up big waves before they hit the coast.

questions.stem: What does “World Heritage Site” mean?
questions.answer: A place so special that the world agrees to protect it
choices: A place where nobody may visit
A place owned by the United Nations
A place that is always hot
questions.explain: UNESCO lists World Heritage Sites — the Great Barrier Reef has been one since 1981.

questions.stem: Burning coal, oil and gas releases which gas that warms the planet and makes the sea more acidic?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat (warming the sea) and dissolves in the sea (acidification).
